deep.reconstruction:
This page contains no mathematics. It is a continuous passage of German historical notes, apparently lecture or reading notes, on the early history of Macedon. It continues directly from the previous page, which covers Amyntas III's sons, Pelopidas, and Ptolemy of Aloros, and it runs on into the next page.

Content, step by step:
(1) Perdiccas III also faced a strong opposing faction led by Pausanias, a prince of the royal house. He held power with Athenian support. In 360 he was killed on a campaign against the Illyrians.
(2) Two claimants to the throne then appeared: Amyntas, a son of Perdiccas, and Philip, a brother of Perdiccas.
(3) Philip came to power in 360 under very doubtful prospects. The Macedonians had just been defeated. Several republics, i.e. the Greek colonies, lay on the coast, and the powerful Greeks were nearby. There were also two further pretenders to the crown.
(4) A character judgement follows: the more fortunate, cautious and circumspect he was, the more courageous he was.
(5) He created a standing army and 'invented' the phalanx, described as heavy infantry with spears 20–24 feet long. The sentence continues on the next page ('langen Spießen bewaffnet…').

There is no derivation, formula or computation. The only numbers are the dates 360 BC and the spear length of 20–24 feet. Nothing on the page bears on mathematics. The handwriting and the subject (school or university ancient history) suggest these are notes taken by a student, possibly not by Gauss himself. They may have been filed in the bundle by accident.
errors: Historical dating: the death of Perdiccas III and Philip II's accession are now usually placed in 359 BC, not 360 BC. Older handbooks often give 360/359.
'Erfand die Phalanx' overstates the case. Philip reformed and developed the Macedonian phalanx, armed with the sarissa, but phalanx tactics existed earlier in Greece.

Sarissa length is usually estimated at about 4–6 m (roughly 13–21 ft). The figure of 20–24 Fuß is at the high end, though it is consistent with some ancient sources (Polybius gives 14–16 cubits for a later period).
